title: Linear reductivity and smoothness of the closure of a semisimple cyclic subgroup
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $H$ be an affine finite-type $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. An algebraic representation on a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $V$ is a group-scheme homomorphism to $\operatorname{GL}(V)$, where $\operatorname{GL}(V)(A)$ is the group of invertible $A$-linear endomorphisms of $V\otimes_k A$. A group is linearly reductive if every finite-dimensional algebraic representation is a direct sum of simple representations; simple means nonzero with no nonzero proper invariant $k$-subspace, and invariant means preserved after every commutative $k$-algebra extension. Let $s\in H(k)$ be semisimple, meaning that its image in every finite-dimensional algebraic representation of $H$ is diagonalizable over $k$. Set $\Gamma=\{s^n:n\in\mathbf Z\}\subset H(k)$. Let $G$ be the reduced closed subscheme of $H$ supported on the Zariski closure of these rational points [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-closed-immersion]; reduced means that its local rings have no nonzero nilpotents. Then the multiplication, inverse and identity of $H$ restrict to $G$, making $G\hookrightarrow H$ a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]; $G$ is smooth over $k$ [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and linearly reductive. Moreover $\Gamma\subset G(k)$ is Zariski dense in the underlying topological space of $G$. No connectedness assumption is imposed on $H$ or $G$.

source.place: Corollary 13.8, printed p.257, first part of its proof (linear reductivity of the cyclic closure); Lemma 1.40, Theorem 1.45 and Definition 1.48, printed pp.18-20, and Proposition 1.26, printed p.13, for its reduced smooth subgroup structure. Semisimple elements and their representation criterion: 9.19, printed p.171.

proof.text: Construct the constant integer group scheme $C=\coprod_{n\in\mathbf Z}\operatorname{Spec}k$. The product $C\times_k C$ is covered by the open-and-closed components indexed by $(n,m)$, each a copy of $\operatorname{Spec}k$; define multiplication there by the component $n+m$, inverse by $n\mapsto-n$, and identity by the component $0$. The group identities hold on each component by the integer identities. Map the $n$th component to $H$ by the point $s^n$. The identity $s^{n+m}=s^ns^m$ makes this a homomorphism $a:C\to H$. With object scheme $U=\operatorname{Spec}k$, these are absolute groupoid schemes and a morphism of them, by [def-a1-groupoid-scheme]. Its topological image is exactly $\Gamma$. No finite-type assertion about $C$ is used.

source.place: Tag 04Q8, lemma-map-groupoids-on-perfect-field-image, applied to the explicitly constructed constant integer group scheme

proof.text: The field $k$ is perfect: in characteristic $p>0$ each $b\in k$ has a $p$th root since $T^p-b$ has a root; characteristic zero is perfect by the stated convention. Apply [lem-sfb-perfect-field-groupoid-image-closure] to $a$. Its reduced image closure is precisely the specified $G$, and its restricted groupoid operations give multiplication, inverse and identity, hence a closed subgroup of $H$. By [def-weil-closed-immersion], writing $H=\operatorname{Spec}B$, we have $G=\operatorname{Spec}(B/I)$. A finite list of algebra generators of $B$ maps to generators of $B/I$, so $G$ is affine and finite type. Each point $s^n$ factors through $G$: every element of $I$ has zero value at that point by the definition of the reduced induced structure. Their set is dense in $|G|$ because $|G|$ is its closure.

The reduced finite-type $k$-scheme $G$ is geometrically reduced by [lem-kun-geometric-reduced-perfect], since $k$ is perfect. It is now a group scheme locally of finite type, so [lem-sfb-geometrically-reduced-group-smooth] shows that $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth. Neither assertion assumes connectedness.

source.place: Tags 047N and 047P, lemma-group-scheme-characteristic-zero-smooth and lemma-reduced-group-scheme-prefect-field-characteristic-p-smooth; geometric reducedness: varieties.tex Tag 020I, lemma-perfect-reduced

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup] to $\mathrm{id}_H$: its kernel is the identity subgroup $1\subseteq H$, which is normal since conjugation fixes the identity on every algebra. Apply [lem-sfb-normal-subgroup-representation-kernel] with this subgroup. This gives a representation $i:H\to\operatorname{GL}_{m,k}$ with $m\geq1$ and trivial kernel on every algebra, hence injective on every algebra. Its restriction $i|_G$ is faithful because the closed immersion $G\hookrightarrow H$ is injective on algebra-valued points. By the hypothesis on $s$, the matrix $i_k(s)$ is diagonalizable. Fix any representation $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$. If $V=0$, it is the empty direct sum of simples. Otherwise choose a basis, put $d=\dim_k V\geq1$, and apply [lem-sfb-rational-representation-semisimple-point] to $J=G$, $i|_G$, $r$ and $s\in G(k)$. Thus $r_k(s)$ is diagonalizable. This step does not assume that representations of $G$ extend to $H$.

source.place: Corollary 5.19, printed p.103, and Section 9.19, printed p.171; the faithful representation bridge implicit in Corollary 13.8

proof.text: Choose an eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $r_k(s)$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j\in k^\times$. In this basis write the universal matrix of $r$ as $(b_{ij})$ with $b_{ij}\in k[G]$. At $s^n$, for every integer $n$, it is $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^n,\ldots,\lambda_d^n)$, including negative $n$ because all eigenvalues are nonzero. For $i\ne j$ the zero locus of $b_{ij}$ is closed and contains the dense set $\Gamma$, hence contains all of $|G|$. In particular $b_{ij}$ vanishes at every $k$-point. Clause (2) of [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] applies to the reduced finitely generated algebra $k[G]$ and gives $b_{ij}=0$. Evaluation at every $g\in G(A)$, for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, therefore makes $r_A(g)$ diagonal. Its inverse is $r_A(g^{-1})$, also diagonal, so each diagonal entry is a unit. Consequently every line $ke_j$ is preserved with equality after every algebra extension, including nonreduced algebras.

source.place: Corollary 13.8, printed p.257: a subspace is stable under the cyclic closure if and only if stable under s; matrix-coordinate verification using schematic density

proof.text: Each nonzero one-dimensional invariant space $ke_j$ has only the subspaces $0$ and itself, so its restricted representation is simple. The basis decomposition $V=\bigoplus_{j=1}^d ke_j$ is equivariant over every algebra by the diagonal calculation. Since $r$ was arbitrary, every finite-dimensional representation of $G$ is a direct sum of simples. This is linear reductivity as defined in the item; together with steps 2 and 3 it proves all assertions.
